item.title: Welcome and Opening Keynote of MLcon Berlin 2026
item.abstract: Welcome and Opening Keynote of MLcon Berlin 2026 by the program chair Sebastian Meyen.

item.title: Hack Me If You Can: Designing Unbreakable LLM Guardrails
item.abstract: Organizations are racing to add generative AI to their applications, but LLMs introduce a new attack surface. Prompt injection, jailbreaks, data leakage, unsafe outputs, and violations of business policy cannot be solved with traditional security controls alone.This keynote explores how to design effective, layered guardrails for GenAI systems, combining prompt-injection detection, content safety, business rules, and input/output controls. We’ll look at how guardrails fail, how attackers adapt, and how observability, red teaming, and continuous evaluation can make defenses stronger over time.The goal is not to build an LLM that can never be broken, but an AI system that expects to be attacked and gets harder to break every time someone tries.

item.title: The Last App: When Software Stops Being a Product
item.abstract: For forty years, an app was a product. You built it once and shipped one version to everyone. That era is ending, not because software is disappearing, but because it is splitting in two.On one side is the "every-app": one AI system that builds whatever you need, shaped to you. Your own budget tracker, your own tools, summoned in a sentence, never finished. This doesn't reduce the software in the world. It multiplies it.On the other side is what the every-app can't replace. It is the most valuable software there is. Some exists so a company has someone to blame when it fails. Some matters only because everyone else is already on it. Some operates where a confident wrong answer is a disaster: payments, healthcare, anything regulated. The every-app takes the easy middle. The hard, valuable edges remain.We've climbed this ladder before: code, then builds, then directing AI. Each step traded typing for judgement. This is the next step. It won't be painless, but the lasting skill was never owning a safe corner. It's seeing the shift early and moving first.For developers and technical leaders curious where software is heading, and where the value goes.

item.title: When Code Becomes Free: The Organizational Bottleneck of the AI Age
item.abstract: What happens when code becomes nearly free to produce, time-to-market approaches zero, and a single engineer ships 20–30 pull requests a day with AI?This talk explores a growing paradox: as AI removes technical bottlenecks, a new one emerges—human judgment and organizational speed. While teams are busy aligning in meetings, AI continues building—often the wrong things, but at scale.Using examples from advanced teams (e.g. Boris Cherny, Claude Code), the session reframes software development in 2026: the challenge is no longer writing code, but making decisions fast enough to keep up. Build to think, not think to build. Ship variants, observe outcomes, and decide based on reality.The real shift for leaders is not prompting—it’s designing decision architectures: turning alignment into infrastructure, decisions into deployed systems, and exploration into a disciplined practice.For engineering, product, and executive leaders navigating the shift from building faster to deciding faster.
